papers.title: BNIP3L/NIX-mediated mitophagy limits Alzheimer’s disease pathology and preserves neuronal function
papers.summary: This paper examines how a mitophagy receptor called BNIP3L/NIX, which tags damaged mitochondria for autophagic clearance, affects Alzheimer's disease progression. The researchers likely show that boosting or preserving NIX-mediated mitophagy reduces disease-related pathology such as amyloid or tau burden and helps maintain neuronal health. This suggests that failure of this specific mitochondrial quality control pathway may contribute to neurodegeneration in Alzheimer's disease.
papers.why: This directly addresses mitophagy's protective role in neurons, a core mechanistic pillar of your PhD project linking autophagy dysfunction to neurodegenerative pathology.

papers.title: ATG9 and ATG2 as lipid managers at the crossroads of autophagy and extracellular vesicle secretion.
papers.summary: This paper discusses ATG9 and ATG2, two proteins that help manage lipids during autophagy, the process cells use to recycle their own components. It highlights a newly recognized connection between these lipid-handling proteins and the secretion of extracellular vesicles, which are small particles cells release to communicate with each other. This suggests that the molecular machinery for self-digestion and for external signaling share overlapping tools and regulation.
papers.why: Understanding how ATG9 and ATG2 regulate lipid flow between autophagy and extracellular vesicle pathways could clarify core mitophagy/autophagy mechanisms in neurons that may also influence perineuronal net remodeling and intercellular signaling in the brain.

papers.title: Histone deacetylase 6 (HDAC6)-mediated α-tubulin (K40) deacetylation and microtubule destabilization disrupt autophagosome-lysosome fusion in PBDE-47-induced neurotoxicity.
papers.summary: This paper investigates how exposure to the environmental toxicant PBDE-47 causes neurotoxicity by disrupting autophagy. The mechanism involves HDAC6 removing acetyl groups from α-tubulin at lysine 40, which destabilizes microtubules. This destabilization prevents autophagosomes from properly fusing with lysosomes, blocking the completion of the autophagic/mitophagic degradation process in neurons.
papers.why: This paper is highly relevant because it identifies a specific molecular mechanism—HDAC6-mediated microtubule destabilization blocking autophagosome-lysosome fusion—that directly informs the mitophagy/autophagy trafficking pathways central to this PhD project on neuronal autophagy.
papers.figure: A figure showing colocalization of autophagosome (LC3) and lysosome (LAMP1) markers with quantification of fusion events under PBDE-47 treatment with/without HDAC6 inhibition, ideally alongside microtubule acetylation status and structure.

papers.title: β-Asarone Alleviates Post-stroke Neuroinflammation and Improves Mitochondrial Quality Via the BNIP3/BNIP3L-dependent Mitophagy Pathway.
papers.summary: This study investigates how β-Asarone, a natural compound, reduces brain inflammation after stroke in an animal model. It shows that β-Asarone improves mitochondrial health by promoting mitophagy, the selective clearance of damaged mitochondria, through the BNIP3/BNIP3L signaling pathway. The result is better neuronal survival and reduced inflammatory damage following ischemic injury.
papers.why: This paper is directly relevant because it examines BNIP3/BNIP3L-dependent mitophagy in neurons following brain injury, offering mechanistic insight and a potential pharmacological tool applicable to the PhD project's focus on mitophagy and autophagy pathways in neuronal health.
papers.figure: A figure showing mitochondrial morphology/mitophagy markers (e.g., BNIP3/BNIP3L and LC3 colocalization) in neurons post-stroke with and without β-Asarone treatment, ideally paired with quantification of mitophagosome formation.

papers.title: Neuronal oxidative stress and mitophagy contribute to microglial inflammation in radiation-induced brain injury.
papers.summary: This study examines how radiation exposure causes neurons to experience oxidative stress, which triggers mitophagy (the clearance of damaged mitochondria). It finds that this neuronal response contributes to inflammation in nearby microglia, the brain's immune cells. The work suggests a neuron-to-microglia signaling pathway that worsens radiation-induced brain injury.
papers.why: This paper directly addresses mitophagy in neurons and its downstream effects on brain inflammation, which is central to understanding neuronal mitochondrial quality control mechanisms relevant to the PhD project.

papers.title: A Guide to autophagy-dependent cell death: concepts, criteria, and mechanisms.
papers.summary: This paper is a guide outlining conceptual definitions, experimental criteria, and molecular mechanisms for identifying autophagy-dependent cell death, a process distinct from mere autophagy occurring alongside dying cells. It aims to standardize how researchers rigorously distinguish true autophagy-driven death from cases where autophagy is merely a bystander or protective response. The guide likely synthesizes consensus recommendations from experts in the autophagy field, similar to other 'guidelines' papers used to improve experimental rigor across labs.
papers.why: Since the PhD project centers on mitophagy and autophagy in neurons, understanding rigorous criteria for autophagy-dependent cell death is essential for correctly interpreting whether observed autophagic/mitophagic changes in neurons or interneurons reflect adaptive turnover or actual cell death mechanisms.

papers.title: NEFL contributes to DJ-1-mediated neuroprotection and autophagic flux regulation in Alzheimer's disease-like injury.
papers.summary: This paper investigates how NEFL (neurofilament light chain) interacts with DJ-1, a protein known for its protective role in neurons, to protect against Alzheimer's disease-like damage. The researchers found that NEFL helps regulate autophagic flux, which is the process by which cells clear out damaged components. This NEFL-DJ-1 connection appears to be important for maintaining neuronal health and could represent a protective mechanism against AD-related injury.
papers.why: This research is relevant because it explores autophagic flux regulation in neurons under Alzheimer's-like conditions, directly connecting to core mitophagy/autophagy themes even without a spatial or interneuron-specific angle.

papers.title: Dibucaine induces autophagic flux and reduces Ser129-phosphorylated α-synuclein in induced pluripotent stem cell–derived neurons with SNCA duplication
papers.summary: This study tests dibucaine, a local anesthetic, on neurons derived from induced pluripotent stem cells carrying a duplication of the SNCA gene, which causes a genetic form of Parkinson's disease. The researchers found that dibucaine boosts autophagic flux, meaning it enhances the cell's ability to clear damaged components through the autophagy pathway. As a result, levels of a toxic, disease-associated form of α-synuclein (phosphorylated at Ser129) were reduced in these neurons.
papers.why: This paper demonstrates a pharmacological approach to enhancing autophagic flux in neurons, directly relevant to the project's focus on mitophagy and autophagy mechanisms that could inform therapeutic strategies for neurodegenerative protein aggregation.
papers.figure: A figure showing autophagic flux markers (e.g., LC3-II turnover with and without lysosomal inhibitors) alongside quantification of Ser129-phosphorylated α-synuclein levels before and after dibucaine treatment.
